QF.id: Analysis of Equity and Debt Instruments_26

question.text: An investment adviser is comparing post-tax returns for a client in the 30% tax bracket who has two alternatives: (1) Invest Rs.10,00,000 in listed equity shares and sell after 14 months for Rs.12,50,000, or (2) Invest Rs.10,00,000 in a specified debt mutual fund and redeem after 14 months for Rs.11,50,000. Which alternative yields the higher post-tax return?

answer.text: Listed equity alternative: post-tax gain Rs.2,34,375; specified debt MF alternative: post-tax gain Rs.1,05,000 — listed equity is better
Listed equity alternative: post-tax gain Rs.2,12,500; specified debt MF alternative: post-tax gain Rs.1,20,000 — listed equity is better
Listed equity alternative: post-tax gain Rs.2,50,000; specified debt MF alternative: post-tax gain Rs.1,50,000 — listed equity is better
Listed equity alternative: post-tax gain Rs.2,18,750; specified debt MF alternative: post-tax gain Rs.1,05,000 — listed equity is better

explanation.text: The Logic: Listed equity (14 months = LTCG under section 112A): gain = Rs.2,50,000; exempt up to Rs.1,25,000; taxable LTCG = Rs.1,25,000; tax = Rs.1,25,000 x 12.5% = Rs.15,625; post-tax gain = Rs.2,34,375. Specified debt MF (always treated as short-term under section 50AA regardless of holding period): gain = Rs.1,50,000; tax at 30% slab = Rs.45,000; post-tax gain = Rs.1,05,000. The listed equity alternative therefore yields a higher post-tax return. The Trap: Wrong choices use the old 15% rate on debt or apply 12.5% to the full equity gain without the Rs.1.25 lakh exemption. The decisive driver is the gap between equity LTCG (12.5% with exemption) and section 50AA treatment of specified debt funds (slab rate, no LTCG benefit). Note: Rewrote option text to refer to the 'listed equity alternative' and 'specified debt MF alternative' instead of 'Option A/B' so the item survives answer-randomisation, and replaced the distributor-flavoured pro-tip with adviser-neutral wording.
